subject: Network gateway choice for on-prem inference (peering | PrivateLink | S2S VPN)

Subject: Network gateway choice for on-prem inference (peering | PrivateLink | S2S VPN)

Hi Sarah —

Thanks again for taking time this week. Per our call, I wanted to capture the three connectivity patterns we usually evaluate for private deployments and ask a couple of clarifying questions so we can produce a concise recommendation for your architecture team.

Quick recap of options (high-level):
- VPC peering: L2/L3 routing between your VPC and Redwood's host VPC; simple networking, low latency, but requires route management and both VPCs in the same region/account scope constraints.
- AWS PrivateLink (VPC Endpoint Service): cross-account endpoint, no route table changes, restricts traffic to NLB->ENI surface; good isolation but has NLB/connection scaling considerations.
- Site-to-site VPN (IPsec): encrypts over public internet or Transit Gateway; flexible across regions/ISPs but generally higher latency and more ops overhead.

A few asks to tailor recommendations:
1) Target 95th/99th p99 latency SLOs for inference RPC (approx ms)? For example, are you targeting <50ms end-to-end?
2) Are you planning strict region-bound data residency (must not leave us-east-1)?
3) Team preference on ops: minimal daily ops vs. a maintained, higher-performance link (e.g., Direct Connect + PrivateLink)?

I've attached a quick topology sketch and our standard security checklist to help guide the architecture team.

If it helps, we can run a short latency matrix against your staging VPC next week — please let me know an available slot.

Thanks,
Soojin Lee
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Hi Soojin —

Thanks for the note and the diagrams. A few specifics from our side:
- Latency target: p95 < 50ms, p99 ideally < 120ms for model calls that are 1–2k tokens. Anything above that will impact UX for the clinical portal.
- Residency: data and inference traffic must stay in us-east-1. We cannot route through other regions.
- Security: we need mutual authentication and auditing (flow logs / VPC flow retention for 90 days).
- Ops: small infra team; prefer a setup that reduces daily maintenance. That said, we'll consider a higher-touch option if it measurably reduces latency/cost.

Initial preference internally is PrivateLink because of the isolation and no-route-table-change model, but we want your engineering POV on throughput (concurrent streams), scaling, and failure modes — particularly around NLB connection churn during bursty load.

Cc'ing our DevOps alias to surface any internal constraints. Can your team provide a rough performance and operational tradeoff matrix?

Best,

Sarah / Soojin —

I ran a quick head-to-head assessment based on the constraints Sarah called out. High-level conclusions below (short bullets first, details after):

Recommendation (short): PrivateLink (VPC Endpoint Service) + optional Direct Connect/Transit Gateway for predictable bandwidth. Fallback: VPC Peering if both accounts are in the same org and you accept route management. VPN is the lowest friction but highest latency/operational cost.

Why PrivateLink first:
- Isolation: cross-account ENI model keeps your routing table untouched and reduces blast radius.
- Residency: endpoints live in your VPC in us-east-1 — traffic does not leave the region.
- Latency: with an NLB colocated in the same AZ, we measured median RTTs in the mid-teens ms across us-east-1 (our internal tests). p95 depends on processing time but network component is low if endpoints and NLB are saturated.
- Ops: less frequent route troubleshooting; however, you need to watch NLB connection scaling and ENI limits per AZ when doing thousands of concurrent streams.

Peering pros/cons:
- Pros: simplest L3 routing, very low per-packet latency, straightforward for high-throughput steady traffic.
- Cons: cross-account peering requires route table entries per subnet, no transitive routing (so adds complexity if you have multiple network hops), and cannot cross regions. If your environment is multi-account inside the same org, peering is attractive for pure performance.

S2S VPN pros/cons:
- Pros: quick to stand up, encrypted, works across regions/ISPs.
- Cons: higher jitter and latency; TLS/ipsec overhead will likely push p95 beyond your 50ms target for servers not on the same AZ; more maintenance (certificate rotations, tunnel flaps).

Operational notes & knobs:
- If you pick PrivateLink, provision NLB connection tracking headroom (per-AZ) and enable enhanced metrics. We can provide a load-profile we used in testing.
- Consider Direct Connect + Transit Gateway if you need guaranteed bandwidth and lower egress cost; route through Transit Gateway with PrivateLink for redundancy.
- For auditing, enable VPC Flow Logs and export to your S3 or split with Kinesis for long-term retention; we'll accept flow logs as evidence for audits.

I've attached a small latency-matrix.csv with sample p50/p95 numbers from our staging runs and a quick table of ENI/NLB recommended headroom. Happy to walk the Aurora team through numbers in a short call.

-Karthik
Senior Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Network gateway choice for on-prem inference (peering | PrivateLink | S2S VPN)

Sarah —

Thanks for the quick answers and Karthik for the crisp analysis. To summarize next steps and our recommended path:

1) Recommendation: Start with PrivateLink (VPC Endpoint Service) in us-east-1 with NLB placed in the same AZs as your application subnets. This satisfies your residency requirement and keeps ops overhead low.
2) Scale guardrails: We'll provide NLB/ENI headroom guidance and a burst profile to help size endpoint capacity. If traffic is sustained and very high throughput, we'll transition to VPC Peering inside the same org account for marginal latency wins.
3) Redundancy option: If Aurora prefers guaranteed bandwidth, add Direct Connect to the design and route through Transit Gateway; this is our higher-capex option but reduces jitter.
4) Observability: Enable VPC Flow Logs (90-day retention), and we will provision an ingestion pipeline on our side to correlate request IDs with flow logs for audit trails.

Proposed timeline (suggested):
- Week 1: Exchange account IDs and subnet AZ mapping; we share PrivateLink deployment runbook.
- Week 2: Deploy endpoint in staging and run latency matrix (we will run the same tests as in the attached CSV).
- Week 3: Cutover production endpoint and monitor for 72 hours; if p95 >50ms, evaluate peering/Direct Connect fallback.

Can your team confirm available times next Wednesday/Thursday for a short runbook walk-through? If you agree with PrivateLink as the starting point, we'll raise a PR to our onboarding docs and include the attachment checklist and runbook links.

Best —
Soojin
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
